title: Factory
summary: Centralize creation when callers should not know concrete classes.

parts.rule: A factory decides which concrete product to create and returns it through an interface the caller understands. Put selection rules and construction dependencies in the factory; keep product behavior in the products. A useful factory returns a ready-to-use object, not an unconfigured shell.
parts.why: If every caller switches on a type and runs the same setup, adding a product requires edits throughout the codebase. Centralized creation keeps callers coupled to the product contract rather than constructors and vendor clients. The pattern adds indirection, so it needs either real selection or non-trivial setup to justify itself.
parts.example: An import service accepts files with csv, json, or xml extensions. Every parser implements DocumentParser.parse(stream). ParserFactory.create("csv") returns CsvParser(delimiter=",", maxColumns=100); create("json") returns JsonParser(maxDepth=20); create("xml") returns XmlParser(entityExpansion=false). The import workflow asks once, then calls parser.parse(stream) without a three-way branch or imports of concrete parsers. Unknown extension "exe" fails at creation with UnsupportedFormat instead of returning null. A test injects a FakeParserFactory whose product records the supplied stream, so the workflow test does not parse a real file. Adding YamlParser changes the factory registration and adds product tests; the import workflow remains unchanged. The division of responsibility matters: the factory chooses and wires JsonParser, but JsonParser still owns JSON token rules. If the application always constructs CsvParser() with no arguments and there is no second implementation, a factory named CsvParserFactory only hides new behind another call. A direct constructor is clearer. In larger systems, a dependency-injection container may assemble the factory itself, but business code should not query the container as a global service locator.
parts.use: Use a factory when runtime input, configuration, or environment selects among products sharing one contract, or when construction must consistently wire several dependencies. Keep it near the composition boundary. Prefer a simple function or registration map before introducing a hierarchy of factories.
parts.refuse: Skip a factory for one trivial concrete type. Do not let the factory become a grab bag of unrelated creation methods or conceal which implementation is running from logs and diagnostics. Return an abstraction only when callers genuinely need that abstraction. An abstract factory for several coordinated product families is a separate, heavier choice and should solve a real compatibility need.

body:
Rule. A factory decides which concrete product to create and returns it through an interface the caller understands. Put selection rules and construction dependencies in the factory; keep product behavior in the products. A useful factory returns a ready-to-use object, not an unconfigured shell.

Why it matters. If every caller switches on a type and runs the same setup, adding a product requires edits throughout the codebase. Centralized creation keeps callers coupled to the product contract rather than constructors and vendor clients. The pattern adds indirection, so it needs either real selection or non-trivial setup to justify itself.

Worked example. An import service accepts files with csv, json, or xml extensions. Every parser implements DocumentParser.parse(stream). ParserFactory.create("csv") returns CsvParser(delimiter=",", maxColumns=100); create("json") returns JsonParser(maxDepth=20); create("xml") returns XmlParser(entityExpansion=false). The import workflow asks once, then calls parser.parse(stream) without a three-way branch or imports of concrete parsers. Unknown extension "exe" fails at creation with UnsupportedFormat instead of returning null. A test injects a FakeParserFactory whose product records the supplied stream, so the workflow test does not parse a real file. Adding YamlParser changes the factory registration and adds product tests; the import workflow remains unchanged. The division of responsibility matters: the factory chooses and wires JsonParser, but JsonParser still owns JSON token rules. If the application always constructs CsvParser() with no arguments and there is no second implementation, a factory named CsvParserFactory only hides new behind another call. A direct constructor is clearer. In larger systems, a dependency-injection container may assemble the factory itself, but business code should not query the container as a global service locator.

[[diagram:create]]

When to use. Use a factory when runtime input, configuration, or environment selects among products sharing one contract, or when construction must consistently wire several dependencies. Keep it near the composition boundary. Prefer a simple function or registration map before introducing a hierarchy of factories.

When to refuse. Skip a factory for one trivial concrete type. Do not let the factory become a grab bag of unrelated creation methods or conceal which implementation is running from logs and diagnostics. Return an abstraction only when callers genuinely need that abstraction. An abstract factory for several coordinated product families is a separate, heavier choice and should solve a real compatibility need.
